https://www.forbes.com/sites/lidiakurasi.text: Leadership Leadership Strategies Poland Seeks To Curb Dependence On Big Tech With "Sovereignty Test" By Lidia Kurasinska , Contributor. Forbes contributors publish independent expert analyses and insights. Lidia Kurasińska covers Eastern European politics and business. Follow Author Jul 21, 2026, 02:16pm EDT Summary Poland is preparing to introduce a mandatory "technological sovereignty test" for major public-sector technology purchases as it looks to reduce dependence on foreign tech providers and strengthen control over critical digital infrastructure. The proposal reflects a broader shift across Europe, where governments are increasingly treating technology as a matter of national security rather than just public procurement. Show More Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks during a news conference following the European Council summit in Brussels on June 19, 2026. (Photo by Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto via Getty Images Poland is preparing to implement a "technological sovereignty test" for major public-sector technology purchases, becoming one of the latest European governments seeking to reduce strategic dependence on U.S. technology providers as governments increasingly treat digital infrastructure as a matter of national security. The proposed mechanism would apply to large public IT projects and assess whether public institutions retain control over critical systems and data while reducing reliance on foreign vendors. The initiative reflects growing concerns that dependence on a small number of foreign technology providers could expose essential public services to political or legal decisions made outside Poland. Rather than eliminating foreign technologies altogether, the government says the goal is to strengthen resilience, maintain operational continuity and give the state greater control over critical digital infrastructure. How the sovereignty test would work Announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the assessment would apply to government technology procurements worth more than 5 million zloty ($1.3 million) and infrastructure projects valued at more than 15 million zloty ($3.9 million). Among other criteria, it would assess the state’s control over a system’s architecture, ownership or access rights to AI model weights, and freedom from vendor lock-in. The greatest threat is "jurisdictional, not technical," says Albert Szczepaniak, director of Security and Quality at Polcom, a Polish data center and cloud services provider. He argues that relying on providers governed by foreign legislation exposes critical infrastructure to external legal regimes, specifically pointing to U.S. laws such as FISA 702 and the CLOUD Act. MORE FOR YOU Under the CLOUD Act, U.S. authorities may request access to data held by American companies even if it is stored on servers located in Europe. Why Poland wants greater technological sovereignty The proposal comes as Poland's dependence on imported digital technologies continues to grow despite being one of the European Union's leaders in the digitalization of public administration. Poland's digital imports increased from 9 billion zloty ($2.3 billion) in 2016 to nearly 48 billion zloty ($12.5 billion) in 2024, growing by an average of 25% annually. Over the same period, digital exports remained largely unchanged at around 3 billion zloty ($780 million), leaving the country with a digital trade deficit of roughly 45 billion zloty ($11.7 billion). Analysts estimate that by the end of the decade, digital imports could exceed the total value of Poland's imports of oil, gas and coal. The cloud computing market illustrates this dependence. Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google together account for more than 70% of Poland's cloud market, limiting competition and increasing reliance on a handful of global providers. Reducing dependence without abandoning U.S. technology Government officials stress that technological sovereignty does not mean cutting Poland off from foreign technology providers. According to recommendations by the Ministry of Digital Affairs and the Future Council, an advisory body appointed by Tusk, completely replacing U.S. technology providers would be neither technically feasible nor economically desirable. Instead, the government aims to build domestic alternatives in strategic segments representing roughly 20% to 30% of the market, including government cloud services, databases and simpler enterprise systems. Officials argue that developing alternatives in these areas would give the state greater negotiating power, improve resilience and keep a larger share of digital spending within Poland. Marcin Wysocki, deputy director of the Cybersecurity Department at the Ministry of Digital Affairs, said technological sovereignty should not be understood as isolation from foreign suppliers, but rather as the state's ability to make informed choices, maintain control over its data, ensure operational continuity and manage technological dependencies. Szczepaniak believes reaching that target is ambitious but achievable within five years. He points to European estimates suggesting that retaining just 15% of current spending on cloud services and software within Europe by 2035 could generate €37 billion ($42 billion) in added value and create more than 460,000 jobs. Public procurement has strengthened Big Tech's grip According to the Warsaw-based Instrat Foundation, Poland’s current procurement model has reinforced dependence on foreign technology providers. In its recent report , 99% of 72 public tenders analyzed directly or indirectly excluded alternatives to Microsoft products, despite procurement rules prohibiting specifications that unnecessarily restrict competition. As a result, domestic and European companies are often limited to acting as resellers of Microsoft licenses rather than competing with their own software. "Lower security, lower resilience, and lower investment in technologies developed in Poland and Europe are the consequences of relying to such an extent on a single supplier from outside the EU," said the report's author, Jarosław Kopeć. He warned that dependence on one provider leaves public administration vulnerable to price increases, service disruptions and the withdrawal of services. Szczepaniak argues a Polish institution buying a “domestic cloud” that simply resells infrastructure from U.S. hyperscalers does not improve technological sovereignty. “The entire supply chain, not the logo on the invoice, should be assessed," he says. A separate report by the Polish Network of Economics argues that digital sovereignty should be treated as a national security issue, with cloud services, government IT systems and public data regarded as critical infrastructure on par with energy and transport networks. Wiesław Wilk, president of the Polish Cloud Association, said continued reliance on technologies outside Poland's control to deliver public services could create long-term strategic vulnerabilities. "In an extreme scenario, losing access to such services could have consequences for the functioning of the state comparable to a disruption in supplies of critical raw materials or energy," he said. A broader European push for technological sovereignty Poland's initiative reflects a broader trend taking shape across Europe, where governments are seeking to reduce strategic dependence on non-European technology providers while avoiding complete technological decoupling. As the relationship with the U.S. has become more uncertain, concerns over the concentration of cloud services among a handful of American companies have grown, alongside efforts to strengthen Europe's technological resilience. In June, the European Commission unveiled its most comprehensive initiative yet to strengthen the bloc’s technological sovereignty. The package aims to reduce Europe's dependence on non-European providers in strategic sectors including semiconductors, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and open-source software. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etim.text: âSince Auschwitz, we know what man is capable of. And since Hiroshima, we know what is at stake.â- Viktor E. Frankl, Austrian psychiatrist, philosopher, and Holocaust survivorItâs been 81 years to this day that the world saw destruction to the extent it hadnât seen before. Rather, they heard it from afar as Enolay Gay dropped Little Boy (worldâs first atomic bomb made of uranium) on Hiroshima, Japan. The ones who bore the brunt of it did not live to tell the tale. Some did, but that existence as history recorded them was âmore painful than deathâ.The next one would be Nagasaki, Japan, on August 9th. That was a plutonium bomb named Fat Man, and this atomic bomb was 40% more powerful than the first one. The world hasnât been the same since. But in some significant ways, the world has also been the same since. Look at how every generationâsince the generation that fought, won or lost the Second World Warâhave always remembered the world-ending possibility of nuclear bombs. And the dangers of totalitarianism.Eight decades have passed but the dangers of both nuclear bombs and fascism are still alive. We may think the world was never as bad as it is today. But the thing is every generation has thought this, and every generation after us will. Because history repeats itself was never really a cliche. None of us have to be students of history or need a PhD to understand that we have always been one step too far or close from some sort of dictatorship because that is the nature of power.Maybe that is the reason why the bombs stopped falling in 1945, but storytellers all over the world have never stopped imagining their consequences. Some writers have recreated the unbearable reality of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to honour the victims and capture the physical horror of atomic warfare. Others have asked what would have happened if the Axis powers had won the Second World War, using alternate history to show how authoritarianism flourishes when armed with ultimate force.The stories that keep humanity awakeStill others build dystopian futures where fascism returns, democracy collapses, or nuclear annihilation hangs over everyday life. Together, these works serve the same purpose: ensuring that humanity never becomes comfortable enough to forget what happens when authoritarianism, militarism, and technological destruction converge.Today, as modern geopolitical tensions reactivate global nuclear anxieties and democratic norms face severe strain, these narratives provide an urgent, simple truth: catastrophe and tyranny are never as far away as we think.The earliest works about Hiroshima were acts of witnessing. They were attempts to preserve human experiences that were impossible to describe. John Hersey's Hiroshima transformed six ordinary survivors into the voices of an unimaginable tragedy, demonstrating that history is understood most profoundly through individual lives rather than casualty figures. Masuji Ibuse's Black Rain explored the lingering physical and emotional scars left by radiation, showing us that the bombing did not end when the explosion subsided. The suffering continued for decades through illness, discrimination and trauma.Cinema carried that responsibility forward. Animated films such as Barefoot Gen and Grave of the Fireflies exposed audiences around the world to the devastation of wartime Japan through the eyes of children. These stories serve as our cultural witnesses. As the generation that survived the bombings gradually disappeared, literature and cinema inherited the responsibility of remembrance. Since then they have become archives of empathy, ensuring that the victims remain people rather than historical abstractions. And the lessons learned are taught again and again.Ray Bradbury and the Western influenceWhile Japanese authors documented the real-world aftermath, Western writers used science fiction to explore the future risks of nuclear weapons. Ray Bradbury stood at the forefront of this movement, creating speculative stories that examined what happens when technological capability outpaces human moral development.Bradburyâs famous 1950 short story, August 2026: There Will Come Soft Rains (published in The Martian Chronicles), presents a world where humanity has been completely wiped out by a nuclear war.Christopher Nolan's 2022 film Oppenheimer approached the story of the atomic bomb from a different perspective. This film examines the scientists who created the atomic bomb, and the moral weight of scientific achievement. While its focus remained far from Hiroshima's streets, it reignited global conversations about whether technological progress can ever be separated from ethical responsibility.Another powerful way storytellers keep the memory of fascism and nuclear danger alive is through alternate history. By exploring what the world would look like if the Axis powers had won World War II, these narratives illustrate how rapidly freedom, truth, and human rights can be erased when authoritarian regimes gain absolute technological and military dominance.Why itâs essential to imagine alternate historiesPhilip K. Dick's The Man in the High Castle, later adapted into an acclaimed television series, imagines an America divided between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan after an Axis victory. Robert Harris's Fatherland presents a Europe where Nazi rule has endured into the 1960s, exposing the machinery of denial and historical revisionism that sustains totalitarian regimes.These stories are not intellectual games built around historical speculation. Their purpose is moral. Modern dystopian fiction brings together the twin threats of radiological catastrophe and political authoritarianism, showing how environmental disasters and nuclear threats can be exploited by extremists to build totalitarian states.Margaret Atwoodâs 1985 novel The Handmaid's Taleâand its modern television seriesâprovides a clear example of this thematic convergence. While Gilead is often understood primarily as a patriarchal, religious dictatorship, the state's rise to power is explicitly triggered by environmental and nuclear destruction.The backstory reveals that widespread infertility was caused by nuclear power plant meltdowns, uncontrolled atomic waste, and toxic pollution. The extremist "Sons of Jacob" movement uses the resulting panic over human survival to overthrow the United States government, suspend the Constitution, and strip citizensâespecially womenâof all basic rights.By imagining worlds where fascism triumphed, they remind us that its defeat was never guaranteed. Democracies survived because millions fought to defend them. Had history shifted only slightly, today's political mapâand perhaps the values underpinning modern societyâmight look terrifyingly different.That lesson resonates deeply in an era when democratic institutions are once again under strain. Across continents, authoritarian rhetoric has found renewed audiences. Fiction cannot predict political outcomes, but it can illuminate recurring patterns. It can remind readers that authoritarianism rarely arrives announcing itself as tyranny. More often, it presents itself as necessity.The British television film Threads remains one of the most terrifying portrayals of nuclear war ever made, depicting not the explosion itself but the slow collapse of civilization in its aftermath. Similarly, the American television film The Day After shocked audiences in the 1980s by presenting nuclear conflict not as heroic spectacle but as an irreversible humanitarian disaster.Stanley Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove approached the same nightmare through satire, exposing the absurdity of military logic capable of ending civilization through bureaucracy, paranoia and technological overconfidence.Even the acclaimed miniseries Chernobyl, though centred on a nuclear accident rather than warfare, examines themes that echo Hiroshima's legacy: secrecy, political denial, institutional arrogance and the devastating human cost of nuclear technology when accountability disappears.Every scientific breakthrough needs an ethical compassThe warnings created by novelists and filmmakers match the real-world appeals made by the scientists who built the first atomic weapons. The history of the nuclear age is defined by an ongoing conflict between scientific discovery and moral responsibility.In 1946, physicist Albert Einstein summarized the danger facing the world in a famous declaration: âThe unleashed power of the atom has changed everything save our modes of thinking and we thus drift toward unparalleled catastrophe.âPolish-born physicist Joseph Rotblat offers one of the clearest historical examples of scientific integrity. Rotblat worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, but he became the only scientist to resign from the project on moral grounds in late 1944.Once it became clear that Nazi Germany had abandoned its own atomic bomb program, Rotblat realized the weapon was no longer being developed purely as a deterrent. Refusing to participate in creating a weapon of mass destruction that could be used for post-war geopolitical dominance, he left the project.For the rest of his life, Rotblat worked toward nuclear disarmament and international peace. In 1955, alongside Einstein, Bertrand Russell, and other prominent scholars, Rotblat co-signed the Russell-Einstein Manifesto. The manifesto presented a direct question to the entire world: âHere, then, is the problem which we present to you, stark and dreadful and inescapable: Shall we put an end to the human race; or shall mankind renounce war?âThe literary testimonies of Hiroshima, the speculative warnings of Bradbury, the alternate histories of Philip K. Dick, the dystopian visions of Atwood, and the moral appeals of Rotblat all connect to form a single, vital message. They demonstrate that nuclear weapons and authoritarian governance are not separate issues; they are twin threats that emerge from the same combination of aggressive militarism, state control, and technological power.These artistic and historical works perform an essential service for modern society. They refuse to let the world treat the atomic bombings of 1945 as distant, forgotten history. By forcing readers and viewers to confront the reality of radiation sickness, the horror of automated post-nuclear landscapes, and the cruelty of fascist regimes, storytellers prevent collective amnesia.They remind every generation that democratic freedom, scientific ethics, and international peace must be actively maintained. And that humanity can never afford to forget what happens when technological power is divorced from human empathy.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/andrew-tate-la.text: Andrew Tate's own lawyers have told a US federal court that the multimillion-pound supercars, private jets and superyacht that built his online brand were largely rented, borrowed or staged.The admission appears in a court filing lodged on behalf of Andrew, 39, and his brother Tristan, 38, as part of their bid for release from a Miami detention centre while they fight extradition to the United Kingdom.The brothers have been held at the Federal Detention Center in Miami since their arrest on 18 July 2026. Their lawyers argue the government has mistaken calculated online performance for genuine evidence of hidden wealth.Lawyers Say Supercars and Yacht Were Rented PropsThe filing, reported by Forbes and other outlets on 25 August 2026, states that vehicles central to the brothers' online image, including a £5.6 million ($7 million) customised Bugatti and a £1.7 million ($2.1 million) Aston Martin, were rented rather than owned.Tristan posted photographs of himself with both cars on social media - posts prosecutors had pointed to as evidence of concealed assets.Lawyers also challenged claims about a superyacht featured in the brothers' promotional videos. 'A promotional video filmed aboard a yacht is not evidence of title to the yacht,' the filing states, per Forbes. 'The "superyacht" does not belong to the Tates.'The brothers' attorneys argue this pattern extends across their online output. The filing states, as reported by Forbes, that it is 'in their interest to portray themselves on social media as uberwealthy', noting that displays of extreme wealth are commercially useful to the brothers' online business model.They Are Playing a Role, Filing ClaimsThe court document goes further than disputing individual assets, framing the brothers' entire wealth-flaunting persona as a calculated performance for engagement and revenue. 'The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point,' the lawyers wrote, per Forbes.'The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role.'The filing lists specific claims the lawyers now describe as exaggeration, including posts suggesting Andrew's tweets alone generate nine-figure sums, that he will one day become UK prime minister, and that he could beat a wolf in unarmed combat. 'All of these posts are hyperbole,' the filing insists.Lawyers also dismissed suggestions that the brothers hold unlimited cryptocurrency reserves or maintain standing access to private jets. They argued such claims were promotional exaggeration used to market Hustlers University, a subscription course once priced at $49.99 a month, and a $5,000 offshore tax programme.Wealth Claims Central to Detention FightThe brothers' online image has taken on direct legal significance because US prosecutors have cited it as grounds to keep them detained pending extradition, arguing that access to vast, partly hidden wealth makes them a flight risk.Prosecutors say the brothers face a strong presumption against bail in international extradition cases, given the scale of the UK charges against them, which include human trafficking and multiple counts of rape and assault involving several accusers.The Tates' lawyers counter that the government has built its flight-risk argument on 'obvious satire, hyperbole and promotion', some of which, they say, was not even written by Andrew personally.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis rescheduled the previously postponed detention hearing for 27 August 2026 to determine whether the brothers remain in custody or are released while the extradition process continues.The brothers deny all charges against them in the UK, Romania and the US.Their attorney, Joseph McBride, has separately argued the pair face safety risks in custody, telling reporters earlier this month that public hostility toward accused sex offenders had put 'a target on their backs' inside the Miami facility.The court's decision on bail will determine whether the Tates remain behind bars in Florida while the UK's extradition request, due by mid-September 2026, is formally assessed by US authorities.

GuruFocus News September 1, 2026 7 min read EL.RO ECEB.F This article first appeared on GuruFocus . Consolidated Revenue: Over RON6 billion, a 24% increase compared to the first half of last year. Consolidated EBITDA: Nearly RON1.1 billion, with a growth of roughly 7.7%. Net Profit: RON457 million, up by 8.6%. Distribution Segment Revenue: Rose nearly 5% to RON2.84 billion. Distribution Segment EBITDA: Decreased by RON42 million, mainly due to unfavorable OpEx. Supply Segment Revenue: Decreased year-on-year by 2%, reaching RON4.3 billion. Supply Segment EBITDA: RON181 million, a recovery from RON58.5 million recorded in the same period of last year. Supply Segment Retail Volumes: Dropped by 9% as the market calibrated. Electricity Market Volume Supplied: Decreased by 8.9%, from 3.71 TWh to 3.38 TWh. Production Segment Revenue: Double-digit increase. Production Segment EBITDA: More than doubled, going from 2 to 7. Green Electricity Production: Almost 21 GWh in the first half, tripling the volume produced in the first half of 2025. Regulated Asset Base: Reached approximately RON8.71 billion in nominal terms by end of June. Network Investments: Put in operation investments worth RON233 million in the first half of the year. Outstanding Subsidies: Stood at RON2.54 billion at the end of June. Group Liquidity: Available in cash and overdraft limits as of June 30, 2026, was RON2,813 million. Total Receivables: Decreased by 6% in the first six months. Warning! GuruFocus has detected 9 Warning Signs with FRA:ECEB. Is FRA:ECEB fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator. Release Date: September 01, 2026 For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript . Positive Points Societatea Energetica Electrica SA ( FRA:ECEB ) reported a strong first half of 2026, with EBITDA up 7.7% to nearly RON1.1 billion and net profit up 8.6% to RON457 million, demonstrating solid financial resilience. The Supply segment showed a significant recovery, with EBITDA jumping to RON181 million from RON58.5 million in the same period last year, driven by a successful pricing strategy post-market liberalization. The Production segment is growing rapidly, with green electricity output tripling to almost 21 GWh in H1 2026, thanks to the commissioning of new photovoltaic parks, and the company has a robust pipeline of 300 MW of solar and wind projects. The company is making strategic investments, including a high-efficiency cogeneration plant in Craiova and expanding into Moldova, which are expected to create synergies and drive future growth. Management has secured a strong financial structure with a EUR1 billion bond program and centralized credit facilities, providing the flexibility to fund its ambitious CapEx program and capture market opportunities. The company expects to recover roughly RON500 million in outstanding subsidies in the near term, following recent legislative changes, which will ease financial pressure on the group. Story Continues Negative Points The Supply segment experienced a 9% decline in retail volumes, reflecting a slowdown in the Romanian economy and reduced national energy consumption, which could pressure future revenues. The Distribution segment's EBITDA decreased by RON42 million due to unfavorable operating expenses, including higher costs for repairs, maintenance, and third-party services. The group's outstanding subsidies owed by the state remain high at RON2.54 billion, creating a significant financial burden and uncertainty despite the expected partial recovery. The Cernavoda nuclear outage has led to higher energy procurement costs, which could negatively impact supply margins in H2 2026, although management expects the impact to be non-material if resolved quickly. The company faces execution risks on its large CapEx program, with potential delays in project completion that could slip into 2027, particularly for distribution network investments. Management declined to provide specific guidance for Q3 2026 EBITDA due to market volatility, indicating uncertainty in the near-term outlook. Q & A Highlights Q : What is the expected timeline for the recovery of outstanding electricity subsidies, and how will the recent legislative changes impact the group? A : Alexandru Chirita (CEO) stated that with the new law in place, the company expects to see the subsidy recovery increase from 40% to 60% within about a month, translating to roughly RON500 million. This will help decrease the overall cost burden on the group, especially on the supply side. There are also discussions with the state about potentially increasing the percentage to 70% by the end of the year, which would further lower financial pressure. Q : How is the company addressing the declining volumes in the supply segment, and what is driving this trend? A : The CEO explained that the decline in supply volumes is primarily a reflection of the overall economic slowdown in Romania, which has reduced national energy consumption. While this impacts the group's results, management notes that performance is still 70-80% above budget expectations. The company remains focused on managing the situation and expects the market to return to a "new normal" over time. Q : What is the company's CapEx outlook for 2026, and are there any risks of delays slipping into 2027? A : The CEO and CFO confirmed that the company expects to meet or exceed its CapEx plan for 2026, particularly in the distribution network. While there may be slight delays in production projects, the distribution segment is on track. The company has a history of exceeding its ANRE-agreed investment plans and intends to accelerate investments, as grid modernization is a top priority. Any minor slippage could be recovered in 2027. Q : What impact will the Cernavoda nuclear outage have on procurement and supply margins in H2 2026? A : The CEO acknowledged that the nuclear outage will have some effect on costs and supply, but it is not expected to be material if the situation normalizes quickly. While energy prices are temporarily higher, there is sufficient energy available on the market. The company is also engaged in legal discussions regarding remedies, but overall, management is not overly concerned about a significant impact on supply results. Q : How is the EUR235 million Craiova cogeneration plant investment expected to be phased, and when will commercial operations begin? A : The CEO stated that the CapEx for Craiova will likely be split over the project timeline, with orders expected to be placed by the end of the year. The company is in discussions with all parties involved and is confident in the project's economics. The plant is strategically important for balancing the group's energy portfolio, and the company has committed to securing district heating for Craiova, with Electrica expected to take over operations after this winter. Q : Can you provide details on the RON106 million corrections and adjustments embedded in the 2026 tariffs? A : The CFO confirmed that the disclosed RON106 million corrections and adjustments fully reflect the 2024 deviations. This is part of the regulatory framework that adjusts tariffs based on past performance and deviations. Q : What level of network losses should be considered reasonable for fiscal year 2026? A : The CFO indicated that network losses are expected to be around 9%, which is in line with the targets set by ANRE. The company is managing losses effectively and remains within regulatory expectations. Q : Following the H1 results, what level of EBITDA does the company expect for the full year 2026, and which segments will drive changes? A : Management stated that the company is currently over budget and expects to remain so for the rest of the year. However, they declined to provide specific guidance on final 2026 values. The production segment is highlighted as a new growth driver, with EBITDA more than doubling, while the supply segment has shown strong recovery. Q : How are network losses and procurement costs being managed in the current environment? A : The CEO clarified that network losses are in line with ANRE targets. Regarding procurement costs, there is a discussion about the recent increase in energy prices due to the nuclear reactor shutdown. The company will analyze post-closing whether procurement costs exceeded ANRE-accepted pricing. For distribution, any overage would likely be capitalized similar to previous energy crisis mechanisms, while supply procurement is a commercial matter. Q : What is the outlook for Q3 2026 EBITDA given the current market volatility? A : The CFO noted that market volatility is expected to continue through August and September, making it difficult to provide a specific Q3 EBITDA guideline. However, the company maintains a positive outlook for the remainder of 2026, with expectations of delivering results above initial projections.
